newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel frees up portion of frozen PLO funds.
newsitem.headline: Israel frees up portion of frozen PLO funds.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu decided on Monday to transfer to the Palestinian Authority about a third of the funds frozen by Israel after a double suicide bombing last month, his spokesman said.
An aide to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat welcomed the decision, calling it a "positive first step".
The United States, which had said Israel's freezing of taxes and customs duties owed to the Palestinian Authority was "counterproductive", also hailed the partial thaw.
"We welcome any Israeli effort to reconcile the Palestinian economy's well-being with their own understandable concerns about security," a U.S. official said.
Israel's Treasury said 42 million shekels ($12 million) would be handed over to the self-rule administration.

In a statement, Netanyahu's spokesman said: "The prime minister decided today in consultation with the foreign and defence ministers to release about 30 percent of the funds Israel held up and transfer it to the Palestinian Authority."

The decision followed what Netanyahu spokesman Shai Bazak called "partial cooperation" by the Palestinian self-rule Authority in the investigation into the July 30 Jerusalem market attack which killed 16 people, including the two bombers.
The statement also cited swift Palestinian action in arresting and sentencing three Palestinians for the murder last week of an Israeli taxi driver in the West Bank town of Jericho.
"Israel still expects strident Palestinian action in the war against the terrorist infrastructure, action that has still not been taken," it said.
After the twin bombing, Israel clamped a security closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip and froze the funds it owes the Authority under a 1994 economic protocol.
An Israeli Treasury spokesman said some 134 million shekels had been frozen. Palestinian officials said Israel kept back some 220 million shekels of the money.
Netanyahu's spokesman said Israel would continue its policy of easing sanctions against the Palestinian Authority in parallel with Palestinian security steps against "terrorism".

Asked about the partial release of funds, Arafat aide Nabil Abu Rdaineh said: "It is a positive first step. We hope the Israeli government will lift the siege measures, including transfer of the remainder of the money owed."

In the Gaza Strip, Palestinian officials said the Authority was blocking the import of non-essential Israeli products such as soft drinks, potato chips, biscuits and cigarettes as part of a self-sufficiency drive spurred by the closure.
The same goods are already produced in Gaza or imported from abroad, the officials said.
Palestinian Trade Minister Maher al-Masri said he and other ministers were putting together a "comprehensive plan to underpin our national economy".
A senior Palestinian official said the proposals would include a selective boycott of Israeli products considered to be "luxury items".

But other Palestinian officials and traders said the effect was likely to be limited because Israel's ban on workers from the West Bank and Gaza had already severely reduced purchasing power in the two areas.
